lesson.title: Nasal cavity and paranasal drainage
lesson.summary: A meatus lies below its corresponding concha.

steps.title: Nasal Cavity and Paranasal Sinuses
steps.body: The nasal cavity extends from nostrils to choanae and is divided by the nasal septum. Its lateral wall has conchae and meatuses that receive drainage from paranasal sinuses and nasolacrimal duct.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Nasal septum: septal cartilage, perpendicular plate of ethmoid, and vomer. Floor: palatine process of maxilla and horizontal plate of palatine bone. Superior meatus receives posterior ethmoidal cells. Middle meatus receives frontal, maxillary, and anterior/middle ethmoidal drainage. Inferior meatus receives nasolacrimal duct. Sphenoidal sinus drains into sphenoethmoidal recess.

steps.title: How do sensory and olfactory regions differ in the nasal cavity?
steps.body: Olfactory epithelium occupies the superior region near the roof and upper septal and conchal surfaces. General sensation over much of the nasal cavity uses trigeminal branches, with anterior-superior and posterior-inferior territories supplied through different routes. Olfactory fibers pass through cribriform foramina, while most general sensory fibers do not. The septal vascular plexus is yet another layer of organization. Smell, irritation sensation and blood supply should therefore be shown separately on a nasal diagram.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: A meatus lies below its corresponding concha. The inferior meatus receives tears through the nasolacrimal duct rather than drainage from a paranasal sinus. Most anterior sinus drainage reaches the middle meatus; posterior ethmoidal cells drain superiorly and the sphenoidal sinus into the sphenoethmoidal recess. The maxillary sinus opening is high on its medial wall, so drainage depends on mucociliary transport, not simply an outlet at the lowest point.
